newsitem.title: BOSNIA: US defence chief Cohen criticises Bosnia poll delay.
newsitem.headline: US defence chief Cohen criticises Bosnia poll delay.

text.p: The U.S. defence secretary on Thursday sharply criticised a new delay in Bosnian municipal elections, calling it another failure by outside civilian agencies helping rejuvenate the war-shattered country.
"I can only say it is disappointing. It will complicate matters," William Cohen said, adding this would not delay the final departure of U.S. forces from Bosnia in mid-1998.

Cohen said the delay by the Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was simply another sign that civilian agencies were not doing their part to end the requirement for military peacekeeping in Bosnia.

"I am disappointed with those who are responsible for setting up and acquiring the (election) monitors, the financial resources in order to allow the elections to go forward," he told a news conference at nearby camp Dobol. "But it will not in my judgement deter us from carrying out the (military) mission until its completion in June of 1998."
He spoke after the OSCE announced the second delay in municipal elections, which had been scheduled for July, until September 13-14.

Cohen had lunch with U.S. troops at camp Dobol near the tense northern Bosnian town of Brcko and was briefed by U.S. General George Joulwan, who commands all NATO forces in Europe, and senior U.S. officers in Bosnia.
He had his picture taken with dozens of American and Russian members of the NATO-led peacekeeping Bosnia force of 31,000 and said he was proud of the job they had done.

But he said that final peace was up to the former warring factions and that Serbs, Moslems and Croats must have a "change of heart" and realise that peacekeeping forces would not remain after mid-1998.
"What they really need to do is stop hoping in some way that this decision is going to be delayed, that we are going to stay. That is not going to happen, " he said.
The secretary, who replaced William Perry in January, is nearing the end of a four-day trip to Germany, Bosnia, Italy and Belgium.
He has stressed repeatedly this week that some 8,000 U.S. troops in the NATO-led force will leave Bosnia on schedule in mid-1998 and not return even if the war broke out again.

Germany and Britain said this week that other peacekeepers will also leave then, although some European officials have predicted that another military force, perhaps sponsored by the Western European Union, could then be sent into Bosnia.
Cohen arrived at nearby Tuzla on a C-17 U.S. military cargo plane from Aviano, Italy, at midday on a warm and sunny day.
"I was planning on snow and mud and a lot of rain. But you pulled out the sun for me," he said.
He was flying later to Rome for dinner and talks with Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta.

The secretary, wearing a leather flight jacket with his name and title on the breast, seemed to enjoy his new role, telling young troops from the First Armoured Division that "You make me very proud to be an American and your secretary of defence. Make sure you take care of each other."
"I had everything -- burger, pizza, eggroll and milk," he said after lunch with the troops in a green mess tent.

Cohen, a defence policy veteran who served 24 years in Congress, said when taking office that the United States could not afford to be the world's chief policeman and peacekeeper while coping with a shrinking military budget and costly modernisation of its cold-war weaponry.

At Camp McGovern he said that civilian authorities had failed to speedily carry out promises to rejuvenate financial and civic infrastructure in Bosnia. He noted that only half of the rebuilding funds provided for Bosnia in the past year had been assigned to specific projects.

Cohen will fly from Rome to Brussels on Friday morning for a day of meetings with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and permanent representatives to the Atlantic Alliance before reutrning to Washington that night.
